description: We are The K' Oirat, a group from Astana, Kazakhstan, who enjoy astronomy, programming and making science accessible. We have skills in web development, Python data processing and machine learning. We make complex space observations accessible tools that can be explored by people. Help make discovery more accessible, join us! Interested teammates in the fields of astronomy, data validation, machine learning and user experience are welcome.
summary:
ASPAN EON is a web tool that helps people explore what changes in the infrared sky. Built for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, it turns real SPHEREx telescope's observations into aligned images, time sequences, and interactive graphs that users can investigate without writing a single line of code, using FITS

Visitors can browse prepared targets or search by sky position, compare observations, and inspect possible movement or brightness changes. We also integrated an experimental convolutional neural network (CNN) that predicts whether an object belongs to a moving, stable, or variable category. Also, users can upload a compatible FITS image and receive a preview and model scores

Our approach brings visual exploration, astronomical measurements, and machine learning into one workflow. Users can examine the evidence behind a result, all while seeing warnings about unreliable measurements. By making observations easier to explore, ASPAN EON helps students, astronomy enthusiasts, and general citizen scientists identify objects, that may be worth looking into!

We believe this work has enormous POTENTIAL. We wish to improve and improve on the current versions, so that people may actually use our tool.
details:
How it works

  • Find observations: Choose a prepared object or search by name or sky coordinates. Our Python server (We currently have Render connected, and we host on GitHub Pages) retrieves POSSIBLE available image cutouts from NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive
  • Prepare images: Our pipeline aligns observations using their sky coordinates, accounts for background light where available, and checks pixel quality flags
  • Compare frames: Explore observations through time-lapse, blink, side-by-side, swipe, difference, and stacking modes
  • Inspect measurements: View brightness and spectral graphs, observation details, and possible changes flagged by our algorithms
  • Check known sources: Use Gaia DR3 and AllWISE overlays or open the surrounding field in the Aladin sky atlas. However, this has its own limitations.

Data and machine learning

Our team collected 2240 SPHEREx FITS observations covering 95 targets, including asteroids, variable stars, comparison stars, and the 5 challenge targets.

(Detectors D1-D6. Data releases DR1 and QR3)

  • We trained a small convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict three catalog categories: moving, stable, and variable
  • We used a 70/15/15 split by object, keeping each object’s observations together to reduce information leakage
  • The selected model correctly classified 11 of 15 test objects, a result on a generally small sample
  • Visitors can upload a compatible FITS cutout! From there, they can get the model scores AND get an image preview. We will improve on this feature in the future, by allowing users to add more and more FITS files, and to be able to analyze them using all the standard tools we already have.

(The CNN predicts categories from image features. Confirming movement or variability DOES require multiple observations, so we present its results as simply experimental suggestions)

Impact & Creativity

Our approach connects existing, automated suggestions with evidence users can explore themselves.
For prepared objects, visitors can examine images, compare observations, inspect measurements, and consider the model’s prediction within the same website

  • Makes astronomical data easier to explore without writing a single line of code
  • Helps students and astronomy enthusiasts understand how changes are investigated
  • Supports the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by helping users identify candidates that are worth to actually check out later
  • Uses guided examples to explain both interesting signals and uncertain results. So everyone can understand how the tool works!

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, and SVG
  • Data processing: Python, Astropy, NumPy, and SciPy
  • Machine learning: PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Jupyter
  • Backend and deployment: FastAPI, Docker, Render, and GitHub Pages

Design Factors Considered

  • Accessibility: Users can explore FITS observations without writing code or installing astronomy software
  • Scientific: Image alignment, wavelength differences, noise, saturation, and quality flags all affect comparisons
  • Fair: We split the ML dataset by object so observations of the same object would not appear in both training and testing
  • Transparency: Model scores and detected changes are presented as suggestions, with limitations & warnings made clear
  • Performance: Small archive cutouts, cached requests, and prepared examples reduce downloads and basically processing time
